description_full: Crawford & Company provides claims management and outsourcing solutions for carriers, brokers, and corporations in the United States, the United Kingdom, Europe, Canada, Australia, Asia, and Latin America. The company provides claims management services to insurance carriers and self-insured entities risk, including property, public liability, automobile liability, and marine insurance; claims management and adjusting services to insurance carriers and self-insured entities from property and casualty insurance company markets; and field investigation and the evaluation and resolution of property and casualty insurance claims. It also offers claims management services, including workers' compensation, liability, and property; death and dismemberment, business travel, life, disability, critical illness, and credit protection claims programs; short and long term disability, family medical leave act, Americans with disabilities act, and state leave claims; legal services, risk management information, and consultative analytical services; loss mitigation services, such as medical bill review, medical case management and vocational rehabilitation; risk management information services; and administration of loss funds established to pay claims. In addition, the company provides managed repair service and outsourced contractor management to national and regional personal and commercial insurance carriers; services to insurance companies on losses caused by all types of natural disasters comprising fires, hailstorms, hurricanes, earthquakes, floods, as well as man-made disasters, such as oil spills, chemical releases, and explosions; staff augmentation that provides temporary staffing resources; and outsourced subrogation claims management, recovery, and consultative services for the property and casualty insurance industry. Crawford & Company was founded in 1941 and is headquartered in Atlanta, Georgia.

Stock-based compensation of $595 per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 6× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity).
financial_summary: Crawford & Company is a small-cap financial services business with a $550M market cap on $1.3B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +2% over the past three years and +1% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 9% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically.

The business throws off $95M in free cash flow — roughly 7 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 5.19× so those profits are backed by real cash.
Accruals are elevated at -10.8% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.7× net debt/EBITDA, and thin 2.4× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 4.5% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 44% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and profit capture is only 0.1× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

Late-cycle dynamics increase the probability of a slowdown
Credit cycles and regulatory capital — losses accumulate invisibly in good years and appear all at once, and the time to worry is when underwriting standards are loosest.
Interest rate regime shifts — a rapid move in rates can invert the yield curve, crush bond portfolios, and trigger deposit flight simultaneously.

sector_tailwinds: Trading at a 45% margin of safety to estimated fair value — a real cushion against errors in the estimate
Market is pricing in lower growth than the company has historically delivered

sect: Its 3% operating margin trails the Financial Services median (29%) by 27pp, so it is a below-average operator in its field.
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.10x its revenue share).
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-12.7% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.02 across 512 companies in the universe; the top four hold 20% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 19% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 9% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 17% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 35% and a beta of 0.87, it moves roughly with the market.
Trading is thin (about $689K a day), below the $1.0M liquidity floor flagged; building a position would move the price.
In past sell-offs it fell 50% in the 2020 crash, 36% in the 2022 bear market and 66% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 45% below its DCF fair value of $21.09, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 32%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $15.49 to $30.15 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Multiples send mixed signals against Financial Services peers: cheaper on P/FCF 5.8 vs 12.9, richer on P/E 21.8 vs 12.2 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 108% above its 10-year median.
The Street target $15.00 on average, 30% above the price.
The price implies 7.7% annual cash-flow growth, 12pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 9% earns above the cost of capital of 7.9%, but the 1pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 3.77).
It converts 7% of revenue into free cash flow.
It earns a 11% return on equity.
It spends 0.4% of revenue on stock compensation.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 2.1% over 3 years, 5.2% over 5 years and 0.5% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.00, a backlog worth 8% of annual revenue and deferred revenue down 4%.
Capex runs only 0.2x depreciation (0.5% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 12, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has missed earnings estimates by 74.0% on average.
own: Insiders own 44.2%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 47%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (17 sales, net $13.8M sold).
It returns 4.5% a year to shareholders (1.9% in buybacks and 2.8% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 15 consecutive years, raising it 8.2% a year over the last five.
people: With about 8,730 employees, each generates about $150K of revenue, 0.3x the Financial Services median.
That works out to $11K of free cash flow per employee.
